cna.title: of: reserved_mem: prevent OOB when too many dynamic regions are defined

scenarios.value:
AV:L - The overflow only runs in __init boot-time fdt_scan_reserved_mem() while parsing /reserved-memory from the bootloader-provided DTB; there is no post-boot syscall, ioctl, netlink, or network-stack path to this code on OF/DT platforms (arm/arm64/RISC-V/ppc/mips/etc.).
AC:L - An attacker who can supply a device tree simply defines more than MAX_RESERVED_REGIONS (64) dynamically-placed /reserved-memory subnodes (size without reg); each extra node deterministically performs another unchecked write past dynamic_nodes[] without races or layout luck.
PR:N - Triggering requires only a crafted device tree delivered at boot (e.g., compromised firmware/OTA image, supply-chain DTB, unauthenticated PXE/TFTP netboot), not privileges on the victim OS; unprivileged local users and user-namespace capabilities cannot reach this __init-only path.
UI:N - Once a malicious DTB is installed, the stack overflow occurs automatically during early_init_fdt_scan_reserved_mem() before userspace starts; no cooperative action by another user or administrator is required beyond normal boot.
S:U - Impact is confined to early-boot kernel stack/memory corruption within the same host kernel; this is not a VM escape, guest-to-host breakout, IOMMU boundary bypass, or other cross-security-authority scenario.
C:H - Each OOB store writes an attacker-influenced FDT node offset past dynamic_nodes[MAX_RESERVED_REGIONS] onto the kernel stack, corrupting adjacent locals and potentially frame/link registers; per kernel guidance, stack OOB writes enable high confidentiality impact.
I:H - This is a stack buffer overflow (CWE-121/787) during __init: repeated int writes past the 64-element dynamic_nodes[] array can corrupt return addresses and control flow in early boot before full hardening, enabling arbitrary kernel code execution.
A:H - Unchecked OOB writes into the boot-time stack typically cause immediate kernel panic/oops during fdt_scan_reserved_mem() (corrupted count/fdt pointers or trashed frame), denying availability on every boot with a crafted or over-limit DT.

descriptions.value:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

of: reserved_mem: prevent OOB when too many dynamic regions are defined

On boot, fdt_scan_reserved_mem() saves each dynamically-placed
/reserved-memory subnode into a local array of size
MAX_RESERVED_REGIONS.

If the device tree defines more than MAX_RESERVED_REGIONS
dynamically-placed regions, fdt_scan_reserved_mem() writes past the
end of the local array.

Add a bounds check that logs an error and skips the excess regions,
restoring the original behavior.

cna.title: s390/zcrypt: Improve EP11 CPRB domain handling with ASN.1 parsing

scenarios.value:
AV:L - The bug is reached only via the ZSENDEP11CPRB ioctl on /dev/z90crypt (or a zcrypt class device node), following zcrypt_unlocked_ioctl() -> zsendep11cprb_ioctl() -> _zcrypt_send_ep11_cprb() -> zcrypt_msgtype6_send_ep11_cprb(); there is no network, USB, or remote packet path.
AC:L - After prep_ep11_ap_msg() ASN.1 validation, an attacker can reliably trigger the flaw with a minimal non-management EP11 CPRB whose payload omits the domain field or uses variable ASN.1 length encodings; the overlay then writes dom_val at a miscalculated offset with no races or victim-dependent state.
PR:L - The ioctl path performs only ap_perms bitmask checks (ioctl/card/queue masks default to all permitted) and no capability or real-root gate; any local user who can open the zcrypt character device can send crafted EP11 CPRBs, which is standard unprivileged local access on s390 systems with crypto hardware.
UI:N - Exploitation requires only the attacker's own ioctl with attacker-controlled CPRB data; no separate victim action such as mounting a filesystem or opening a file is needed beyond the attacker's direct device access.
S:U - The out-of-bounds write corrupts kernel heap memory inside the zcrypt driver's AP message buffer within the same kernel security domain; it does not cross a VM, container, or IOMMU boundary to impact a separate authority.
C:H - The unchecked struct overlay can write four bytes past the validated ASN.1 payload boundary inside a kernel-allocated AP message buffer; such heap corruption is exploitable for kernel memory disclosure and is scored as high confidentiality impact per memory-corruption guidance.
I:H - zcrypt_msgtype6_send_ep11_cprb() performs an out-of-bounds 32-bit write of AP_QID_QUEUE() via payload_hdr->dom_val when ASN.1 layout does not match the assumed fixed pld_hdr overlay, enabling heap corruption and potential arbitrary kernel code execution.
A:H - Writing past the validated EP11 CPRB payload into kernel heap memory can cause immediate kernel oops/panic or sustained denial of service through repeated ioctl-triggered corruption on IBM Z systems using EP11 crypto adapters.

descriptions.value:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

s390/zcrypt: Improve EP11 CPRB domain handling with ASN.1 parsing

The zcrypt_msgtype6_send_ep11_cprb() function uses fragile struct
overlays to access and modify the domain field in the EP11 CPRB
payload, creating maintainability and security concerns:
1. Struct overlay approach (pld_hdr) assumes fixed payload structure
   and doesn't validate the actual ASN.1 encoding.
2. Complex length format detection logic is error-prone and doesn't
   properly validate bounds at each parsing step.
3. Direct struct member access bypasses proper ASN.1 validation.

Fix by replacing struct overlays with explicit ASN.1 parsing that
validates each field (payload tag/length, function tag/length/value,
optional domain tag/length/value) with proper bounds checking at every
step. Add asn1_int_encode() helper function to safely write integer
values with correct endianness conversion. This makes the code
consistent with the validation pattern introduced with the rework of
the xcrb_msg_to_type6_ep11cprb_msgx() function.

cna.title: bestzip before 2.2.6 and 3.0.x before 3.0.2 Argument Injection via Missing Option Delimiter

references.name: VulnCheck Advisory: bestzip before 2.2.6 and 3.0.x before 3.0.2 Argument Injection via Missing Option Delimiter

descriptions.value: bestzip builds the argument list for the system zip utility without separating options from operands. The destination archive path and the caller-supplied source paths are passed to the child process with no -- delimiter between them, so any source entry beginning with a hyphen is interpreted by zip as an option rather than a file name. zip accepts -T to test the finished archive and -TT to name the command used to perform that test, so a source list containing those two entries and a command string causes zip to run that command through a shell once the archive has been written. An application that passes a file name or path it received from an untrusted source into the bestzip API therefore executes a command of the supplier's choosing. Versions 2.2.6 and 3.0.2 add the delimiter.

descriptions.description: Improper Neutralization of Argument Delimiters in a Command ('Argument Injection')

cna.title: Bluetooth: hci_sync: hold conn in hci_connect_acl/le_sync() callbacks

scenarios.value:
AV:A - Bluetooth HCI outgoing ACL/LE connection setup (hci_connect_acl_sync/hci_connect_le_sync) is driven by adjacent radio peers supplying HCI events (connection complete/failures, command status) while hci_cmd_sync_work blocks on controller replies on phones and laptops.
AC:L - Race between hci_cmd_sync_work using a bare hci_conn pointer and hci_conn_del/hci_conn_failed/create_le_conn_complete teardown; attacker controls both sides by concurrently initiating L2CAP/MGMT connects and aborting or inducing remote HCI failure events until the window hits.
PR:N - Adjacent Bluetooth peers need no Linux credentials; freeing runs on unauthenticated HCI connection events, and local triggering works via unprivileged AF_BLUETOOTH L2CAP connect() without CAP_NET_ADMIN or special namespaces.
UI:N - Background Bluetooth auto-reconnect, pairing flows, or listening socket-driven outgoing connects create BT_OPEN hci_conn objects without deliberate user action; attacker timing of connect/teardown does not require social engineering.
S:U - Kernel heap UAF within the Bluetooth stack enables local privilege escalation in the same kernel domain but does not cross VM, IOMMU, or sandbox boundaries.
C:H - Freed struct hci_conn is dereferenced in hci_acl_create_conn_sync, hci_le_create_conn_sync, and create_le_conn_complete (e.g., conn->pkt_type, conn->dst, conn->le_conn_timeout), enabling slab reuse and arbitrary kernel memory disclosure.
I:H - Post-free writes occur to conn fields (state, flags, timers) and function-pointer members (cleanup, connect_cfm_cb), providing groomable heap corruption suitable for arbitrary kernel write and code execution.
A:H - UAF during hci_cmd_sync_work on connection setup reliably causes kernel oops/panic and can be retriggered by repeated connect/abort cycles from adjacent or local attackers.

descriptions.value:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

Bluetooth: hci_sync: hold conn in hci_connect_acl/le_sync() callbacks

There is theoretical UAF if the conn is freed while the hci_sync task
is running.

Hold refcount to avoid that.

cna.title: hwmon: (asus_atk0110) Check package count before accessing element

scenarios.value:
AV:L - atk_ec_present() runs only during local asus_atk0110 platform-driver probe (boot or module load) when ACPI evaluates the GGRP method; there is no network, wireless, or USB packet path to this hwmon parser on x86 ASUS motherboards.
AC:L - A GGRP sub-package with package.count==0 deterministically indexes elements[0] past the ACPICA allocation on every probe; no race, heap layout lottery, or other attacker-uncontrollable conditions are required once malformed firmware data is present.
PR:N - Malformed ACPI GGRP packages are returned by system firmware and parsed automatically during driver probe without Linux authentication or capability checks; a supply-chain or evil-maid compromised ASUS BIOS suffices with no local account or namespace privilege at trigger time.
UI:N - Exploitation requires no victim interaction beyond normal power-on and boot; the vulnerable enumeration executes automatically when the ATK0110 ACPI device probes and does not depend on another user opening files or mounting filesystems.
S:U - The out-of-bounds read and any resulting EC misconfiguration or kernel fault remain within the host kernel and local ASUS firmware context; this is not a VM escape, container breakout, or IOMMU boundary crossing.
C:H - Accessing elements[0] on a zero-count ACPI package performs an out-of-bounds kernel heap read of a full union acpi_object, exposing adjacent slab contents interpreted as type and integer fields rather than a strictly bounded few-byte disclosure.
I:H - Heap-adjacent data misread as ATK_EC_ID can make atk_ec_present() succeed and drive atk_ec_ctl()/SITM to enable or disable the embedded controller, giving attacker-influenced hardware state modification beyond a read-only fault.
A:H - Reading past a zero-length ACPICA package allocation can dereference invalid adjacent memory and oops or panic the kernel during probe, and repeated reboots on affected ASUS systems cause persistent denial of service until firmware or the driver is fixed.

descriptions.value:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

hwmon: (asus_atk0110) Check package count before accessing element

atk_ec_present() walks the management group package returned by the GGRP
ACPI method and, for each sub-package, reads its first element:

	id = &obj->package.elements[0];
	if (id->type != ACPI_TYPE_INTEGER)

without checking that the sub-package is non-empty.  ACPICA allocates the
element array with exactly package.count entries, so for a sub-package
with a zero count this reads past the allocation.

The sibling function atk_debugfs_ggrp_open() performs the same access but
skips empty packages with a package.count check first.  Add the same
check to atk_ec_present() so a malformed firmware package cannot trigger
an out-of-bounds read.

cna.title: drm/amdgpu: Fix UVD decode image min size calculation

scenarios.value:
AV:L - Reachable only via AMDGPU_CS ioctl on a local DRM render node (/dev/dri/renderD*), through amdgpu_cs_ioctl → amdgpu_cs_patch_ibs → amdgpu_uvd_ring_parse_cs → amdgpu_uvd_cs_pass2 → amdgpu_uvd_cs_msg → amdgpu_uvd_cs_msg_decode; not reachable from any network-facing kernel service.
AC:L - An attacker with render-node access fully controls UVD decode message fields (width, height, pitch in msg[28], stream_type) in their own BO and can reliably set pitch > width (only width > pitch was rejected) to force an underestimated buf_sizes[0x2] check.
PR:L - Exploitation requires only standard unprivileged local access to the AMDGPU DRM render node (DRM_AUTH|DRM_RENDER_ALLOW on AMDGPU_CS ioctl), not real root; user namespaces alone do not grant render-node access.
UI:N - No victim interaction is required; a local attacker can directly craft and submit a UVD command stream with a decode message via AMDGPU_CS ioctl after creating a valid UVD session handle.
S:U - Impact is confined to the kernel/GPU driver on the local host (GPU out-of-bounds access within the attacker's DRM client address space); it does not cross VM, IOMMU, or sandbox boundaries to a different security authority.
C:H - Underestimating the decode image minimum size lets undersized buffers pass amdgpu_uvd_cs_pass2 validation while the UVD engine decodes using pitch stride, enabling out-of-bounds reads of adjacent GPU-mapped memory that may contain sensitive data.
I:H - Using image_size (width-based) instead of (pitch*height)*3/2 for buf_sizes[0x2] allows the UVD hardware to perform large out-of-bounds writes past the validated buffer when pitch exceeds width, corrupting adjacent GPU-mapped memory.
A:H - Large GPU out-of-bounds writes from the UVD decode engine can hang or reset the GPU driver and may trigger kernel oops/panic; unbounded pitch before the fix also risked integer overflow wrapping the minimum size to near-zero, amplifying corruption.

descriptions.value:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

drm/amdgpu: Fix UVD decode image min size calculation

This needs to use pitch instead of width. Also reject pitch
over 4096 to avoid overflow.

cna.title: block: stop the timeout timer when releasing a never added disk

scenarios.value:
AV:N - Exploitation reaches disk_release() via NVMe namespace probing that issues pre-add_disk I/O (FDP io-mgmt-recv, Report Zones) over NVMe-oF TCP/RDMA; a remote or storage-network peer can supply crafted responses during automatic scan/reconnect on cloud/datacenter initiators.
AC:L - An attacker controlling the NVMe endpoint can reliably time namespace enumeration I/O (arming q->timeout) with a concurrent probe failure (controller reset/NVME_CTRL_FROZEN or device_add_disk failure); FuzzNvme made this deterministic, and the attacker controls both sides of the race.
PR:N - No local account or capability is required on the victim host at exploitation time; once an NVMe fabric path exists, a remote/compromised target or storage-network attacker can trigger the probe-failure teardown without CAP_SYS_ADMIN, ioctl, or sysfs access.
UI:N - The bug fires during automatic kernel namespace scan/reconnect and queue teardown on probe failure; no victim mount, login, or manual device interaction is required beyond normal background storage enumeration.
S:U - Impact is kernel slab corruption and crashes within the host kernel block layer; it does not cross a VM, container, or IOMMU security boundary even though virtio_blk shares the same pre-add_disk probe pattern.
C:H - KASAN reports slab use-after-free with an 8-byte write in detach_if_pending on a freed request_queue whose timeout timer remains on the timer wheel; UAF of queue/timer structures enables arbitrary kernel memory disclosure primitives.
I:H - The dangling timer wheel entry corrupts kernel heap metadata and can affect unrelated queues (e.g., ctrl->admin_q in the reported stack); UAF on request_queue/timer state is exploitable for arbitrary write and control-flow hijacking, not merely a crash.
A:H - Observed impact includes KASAN BUG/oops from timer deletion and queue sync on freed memory; leaked timers also trip in enqueue_timer(), __run_timers(), and blk_mq_timeout_work(), causing kernel panics and denial of service.

descriptions.value:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

block: stop the timeout timer when releasing a never added disk

disk_release() undoes blk_mq_init_allocated_queue() for a disk whose
probe failed before add_disk(), but it only calls blk_mq_exit_queue().
Nothing there stops q->timeout, and that timer rolls forward: it stays
pending until it next expires, not until the last request completes.
So if the driver issued any I/O before adding the disk, the
request_queue is freed while still linked into a timer wheel bucket.

Commit 6f8191fdf41d ("block: simplify disk shutdown") dropped the
blk_cleanup_queue() call that used to stop it.  __del_gendisk() and
blk_mq_destroy_queue() still do; only the probe failure path lost it.

nvme gets there because nvme_update_ns_info() submits Report Zones or
FDP io-mgmt-recv on ns->queue before the disk is added, so a later
failure - a concurrent reset setting NVME_CTRL_FROZEN, or
device_add_disk() failing - lands in put_disk() with the timer armed:

  BUG: KASAN: slab-use-after-free in detach_if_pending+0x30c/0x340
  Write of size 8 at addr ffff888004d71310 by task kworker/u8:2/37
   __timer_delete_sync+0x156/0x240 kernel/time/timer.c:1621
   blk_sync_queue+0x22/0x40 block/blk-core.c:222
   nvme_sync_queues+0x100/0x150 drivers/nvme/host/core.c:5362
   nvme_reset_work+0x138/0x930 drivers/nvme/host/pci.c:3264

  Allocated by task 34:
   __blk_mq_alloc_disk+0x33/0x100 block/blk-mq.c:4462
   nvme_alloc_ns+0x290/0x3870 drivers/nvme/host/core.c:4146

  Freed by task 0:
   blk_free_queue_rcu+0x3a/0x50 block/blk-core.c:254
   rcu_core+0xc10/0x1730 kernel/rcu/tree.c:2857

The queue being synced there is ctrl->admin_q, only a victim sharing a
timer wheel bucket with the freed queue's dangling entry; other runs
tripped in enqueue_timer(), __run_timers() or blk_mq_timeout_work().
Failing nvme_alloc_ns() with a debug patch makes it deterministic: one
leaked timer trips KASAN within seconds, while 1987 patched releases
produced no splat.

Stop the timer and the queue work items before blk_mq_exit_queue(), like
blk_mq_destroy_queue() does.

cna.title: Ansible-collection-community-general: community.general: ipa_getkeytab does not set no_log on the bind_pw parameter, disclosing the ipa bind password in logs and process listings

credits.value: Red Hat would like to thank Arpit Jain (GitHub handle: arpitjain099) for reporting this issue.

workarounds.value: Mitigation for this issue is either not available or the currently available options do not meet the Red Hat Product Security criteria comprising ease of use and deployment, applicability to widespread installation base, or stability.

descriptions.value:
A flaw was found in the ipa_getkeytab module of the community.general
Ansible collection. The module's bind_pw parameter, used to supply the LDAP simple-bind password when retrieving a Kerberos keytab, is not declared with no_log, unlike the sibling password parameter in the same module. As a consequence, the supplied IPA/LDAP bind password is recorded in cleartext in the managed host's system journal/syslog (the module's "Invoked with" record), is included in the module's return values and verbose (-v) output, and is displayed in Automation Controller / AWX job output. The password is additionally passed on the command line to the ipa-getkeytab helper (as --bindpw <value>), exposing it in the process list to local users while the command runs. An attacker able to read these logs, job output, or the process table can obtain the directory bind credential, potentially compromising the accounts and objects that credential can access.

cna.title: batman-adv: gw: acquire ethernet header only after skb realloc

scenarios.value:
AV:A - The bug is hit only in batadv_interface_tx on outgoing bat0 traffic; the highest-impact path is an unauthenticated client on the same WiFi/LAN segment bridged to a batman-adv gateway node sending a crafted VLAN-tagged DHCP packet into bat0.
AC:L - Triggering is synchronous and attacker-controlled: a VLAN-tagged DHCP discover/request shaped to force pskb_may_pull() skb reallocation deterministically hits the stale ethhdr UAF without races or victim-specific timing.
PR:N - No privileges on the mesh router are required when a client on a bridged WiFi/LAN port injects the malicious DHCP frame; gateway-client mode is operator configuration, not an attacker privilege.
UI:N - Exploitation requires no victim interaction beyond normal always-on mesh bridging and DHCP forwarding; the attacker only sends a malicious frame.
S:U - Impact is kernel memory corruption and potential privilege escalation within the same kernel/host security boundary, not a cross-boundary escape such as VM or sandbox breakout.
C:H - This is a use-after-free read: after skb reallocation, ethhdr->h_source/h_dest dereference freed skb head memory, enabling uncontrolled kernel memory disclosure and further exploitation primitives.
I:H - UAF on skb data can corrupt routing lookups (batadv_transtable_search) and adjacent kernel heap state, providing a standard path to controlled writes and arbitrary kernel code execution.
A:H - Reading freed skb memory via ethhdr commonly causes kernel oops/panic on the batman-adv gateway node, yielding complete loss of mesh connectivity and host availability.

descriptions.value:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

batman-adv: gw: acquire ethernet header only after skb realloc

The pskb_may_pull() called by batadv_get_vid() could reallocate the buffer
behind the skb. Variables which were pointing to the old buffer need to be
reassigned to avoid an use-after-free.

cna.title: libceph: Avoid using invalid osd indices from primary_temp

scenarios.value:
AV:N - Malformed primary_temp data arrives in CEPH_MSG_OSD_MAP over TCP from a Ceph monitor (mon_dispatch) or OSD (osd_dispatch); calc_target() then uses the bogus osd index in lookup_create_osd()/reopen_osd() to index osd_addr/osd_state/osd_weight without any local syscall.
AC:L - A compromised or malicious monitor/OSD can publish an incremental osdmap whose primary_temp sets an osd index >= max_osd for a victim PG; once applied, calc_target() on pending I/O, linger requests, or map-driven resends deterministically uses that invalid index.
PR:N - The attacker acts as the remote Ceph cluster peer delivering forged osdmaps to an already-connected kernel CephFS/RBD client and needs no local account, capabilities, or user-namespace privileges on the victim host.
UI:N - Once a kernel Ceph client session exists, osdmap updates are applied automatically and scan_requests/kick_requests recalculate targets without any mount, open, or other victim interaction at exploit time.
S:U - Impact is confined to kernel libceph client memory and state on the Ceph client host (heap disclosure, misrouted connections, crash); it does not cross VM, IOMMU, or container sandbox boundaries to another security authority.
C:H - Invalid acting.primary indexes past the end of kmalloc-backed osd_addr, osd_state, and osd_weight arrays, performing out-of-bounds reads of adjacent kernel heap memory that can disclose pointers and other sensitive data.
I:H - Attacker-chosen osd indices drive out-of-bounds reads whose results are treated as authoritative OSD addresses and state for ceph_con_open() and request routing, corrupting kernel client connection targeting in ways usable for further exploitation.
A:H - Out-of-bounds reads with large crafted osd indices can fault on unmapped kmalloc slack and trigger kernel oops or panic; misrouted linger and I/O requests also cause persistent, repeatable client failure on each malicious osdmap update.

descriptions.value:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

libceph: Avoid using invalid osd indices from primary_temp

A corrupted osdmap received from a Ceph monitor or OSD may contain osd
indices in its pg_temp, primary_temp, pg_upmap, and pg_upmap_items parts
that don't exist, i.e., that are greater than max_osd or smaller than
CEPH_HOMELESS_OSD (-1). These indices are used to create the up and
acting set in ceph_pg_to_up_acting_osds(), called from calc_target().
While most of these osd indices are checked, the one from primary_temp
is not. Subsequently, this may lead to calc_target() returning this
(potentially invalid) index as target osd for a (linger) request.
Because the osd_state, osd_weight, and osd_addr arrays only contain
max_osd entries (with indices 0 to max_osd -1), this leads to
out-of-bounds accesses when trying to read values from these arrays.

This patch fixes the issue by adding a check to get_temp_osds(), so that
only valid osd indices from primary_temp are used, and it falls back to
using the primary from pg_temp or the up set if it is invalid.

cna.title: Lantronix Autonomous Out-of-Band Devices Arbitrary File Write via Upload Filename Validation Bypass

descriptions.value: Lantronix SLC8000 before firmware v9.7.0.5, SLC9000 before firmware v9.7.0.2, EMG8500/EMG7500 before firmware v9.7.0.1, and all firmware versions of SLB882/SLCx-03/SLCx-02 contain a path traversal vulnerability in the web management portal upload endpoint that allows authenticated attackers to write arbitrary data to any location on the device's filesystem, leading to remote code execution. The upload filename validation strips backslash characters but does not subsequently check for forward slashes when a backslash is detected; by supplying a filename containing both characters an attacker writes outside the intended upload directory to any writable path. Attackers can use this vulnerability to achieve complete loss of confidentiality, integrity, and availability on the affected device and potentially impact downstream serial-connected devices.

cna.title: EUC_JISX0213 decoding may hang on crafted input

credits.value: AISLE in partnership with Red Hat

descriptions.value: CAPEC-153 Input Data Manipulation

Converting crafted EUC_JISX0213 input to UCS-4 or the internal wide character encoding, for example with iconv, in the GNU C Library version 2.3 to 2.44 may result in the converter making no progress, causing the calling application to hang.

Some EUC_JISX0213 sequences decode to two code points.  If the output buffer has room for only the first one, the converter stores the second in the conversion state and returns E2BIG, but it never clears that pending character after emitting it on the next call.  The converter then keeps emitting the pending character without consuming further input, so an application that retries the conversion loops forever. The input must be attacker controlled and the application must convert it with an output buffer small enough to split the two code points. Only the EUC_JISX0213 character set is affected, which is not commonly used.  The related defect in SHIFT_JISX0213 converter is tracked separately as CVE-2026-77117.

cna.title: OpenSSL pinning bypass

x_osv.details:
When `CURLOPT_PINNEDPUBLICKEY` is configured alongside options that disable
standard peer verification (`CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYPEER = 0` and
`CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYHOST = 0`), libcurl fails to enforce public key pinning on
connections established without a presented server certificate. Bypassing the
pinning check under these disabled-verification conditions allows
unauthenticated connections to succeed when they should be rejected.

cna.title: CMB2 < 2.13.0 - Subscriber+ Arbitrary Option Corruption via oEmbed Handler

descriptions.value:
The CMB2 WordPress plugin before 2.13.0 does not perform any capability check on one of its AJAX actions, allowing users with a role as low as Subscriber to create arbitrary WordPress options and corrupt existing ones, which can break core site settings and take the site offline.
Exploitation requires the site's  or another CMB2 WordPress plugin before 2.13.0 to have declared an oEmbed field, as the CMB2 WordPress plugin before 2.13.0 registers none of its own. The stored value is never attacker-controlled, so the issue does not lead to privilege escalation.

cna.title: Kimai before 2.56.0 Authorization Bypass via TimesheetVoter

references.name: VulnCheck Advisory: Kimai before 2.56.0 Authorization Bypass via TimesheetVoter

descriptions.value: Kimai before 2.56.0 does not enforce team-membership checks in TimesheetVoter::voteOnAttribute(), which maps permissions only to own_timesheet or other_timesheet. As a result, any authenticated user with ROLE_TEAMLEAD (or a role holding edit_other_timesheet/delete_other_timesheet) can read, modify, and permanently delete timesheets belonging to any user system-wide via the API, regardless of team membership. Timesheet IDs are sequential integers and trivially enumerable. ROLE_USER accounts are correctly restricted. (Note: the maintainers characterize this behavior as matching the documented permission model.)

cna.title: drm/amdgpu: reject oversized IBs with per-ring packet limits

scenarios.value:
AV:L - The bug is reached only through the AMDGPU_CS DRM ioctl on a local /dev/dri/renderD* render node; amdgpu_cs_p2_ib() takes user-supplied ib_bytes from command-submission chunks during local GPU job setup, with no network, adjacent-radio, or physical-access path to this code.
AC:L - An attacker fully controls ib_bytes, ring selection, and backing BO mappings in each submit; triggering the flaw only requires one crafted IB chunk with length_dw above the hardware 20-bit packet limit (e.g., >0xFFFFF dwords), with no race or victim-dependent timing.
PR:L - AMDGPU_CS is registered with DRM_AUTH|DRM_RENDER_ALLOW, so any authenticated render-client process with standard local access to /dev/dri/renderD* (typical render/video group on desktops, gaming PCs, and cloud GPU VMs) can reach amdgpu_cs_ioctl() without real root or init-namespace capabilities.
UI:N - Exploitation is entirely self-contained in the attacker's own DRM client (open render node, allocate/map buffers, submit CS); no separate victim action such as opening a file, mounting a filesystem, or clicking a link is required.
S:C - On GFX/compute rings, ring_emit_ib() ORs ib->length_dw into the INDIRECT_BUFFER control dword alongside VMID and preempt/valid bits; oversized values spill into those fields, so the GPU can execute IBs under an unintended VMID and perform DMA outside the attacker's GPU virtual address space, crossing per-client GPU/IOMMU isolation (e.g., multi-tenant cloud GPU).
C:H - Corrupted VMID and adjacent control bits in the INDIRECT_BUFFER packet can redirect GPU fetches/execution into another client's GPU-mapped memory, providing a cross-context read primitive beyond the attacker's own BO mappings, not merely a benign driver error return.
I:H - The same control-dword overflow can alter VALID/PREEMPT/VMID encoding so the GPU performs writes and command execution in an unintended address space, yielding cross-context memory corruption and a plausible path to arbitrary GPU-visible memory modification or further kernel compromise.
A:H - Oversized IB lengths also destabilize command submission and can hang or reset GFX/SDMA rings (as noted in the fix and related IGT oversize-packet tests), denying GPU/display availability until driver reset or reboot on affected AMD systems.

descriptions.value:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

drm/amdgpu: reject oversized IBs with per-ring packet limits

On GFX rings, amdgpu_cs_p2_ib() passed user-supplied ib_bytes through
to ib->length_dw without a limit, while ring_emit_ib() encodes length
into packet fields. Oversized values can corrupt adjacent control bits
and destabilize command submission.

Add a per-ring IB packet size limit helper and reject command
submissions exceeding the corresponding dword limit before IB
allocation. Use the documented 20-bit limit for GFX/compute/SDMA/VPE,
and apply the MM fallback limit for other ring types.

descriptions.value: Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 5.1.0 until 13.0.0, Pillow can exhaust resources while parsing an existing PDF during an append operation. PdfParser follows page-tree child references without cycle or duplication tracking and follows previous-trailer chains with only an exact repeated-offset guard, so deep or cyclic page trees and long chains of unique trailer offsets can exhaust the Python stack. Repeated non-cyclic /Kids references can also cause super-linear CPU and memory use. An attacker can supply such a PDF to an application that calls Image.save with PDF append enabled. This can raise an uncaught RecursionError or consume excessive CPU and memory before output is written, causing denial of service. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

ai_annotations.description: Draft vulnerability metadata was generated from a git-format patch using an Ollama-hosted language model. Human validation is required before publication.

patches.subject: fix: [sync] Only use a valid colour for remote tags in the

x_patch2vuln.subject: fix: [sync] Only use a valid colour for remote tags in the
x_patch2vuln.fixSummary: The fix introduces strict validation of the tag colour value before it is rendered into a CSS style attribute. Only values matching a valid six-digit hexadecimal colour pattern (e.g. #aabbcc) are accepted; any other value is replaced with a safe default (#ffffff). This prevents arbitrary CSS from being injected through the colour field, aligning the remote tag handling with the validation already applied to local tags.
assumptions: The affected version boundary is inferred from the tag_version_boundary metadata (v2.5.48, 27 commits after fix); the exact first affected version is not stated in the patch.
PR:L assumes that creating or modifying a tag on a linked MISP server requires only low-level user privileges; the exact permission model was not verified from the patch.
SC:L assumes CSS injection could enable limited client-side information disclosure (e.g., via CSS selectors or layout manipulation); full XSS or data exfiltration is not evidenced.
CAPEC-66 is the closest available mapping; no CAPEC specifically models CSS injection via trusted inter-instance data, so this mapping carries uncertainty.
The commit message states the issue was found during internal review and not externally reported; no external finder or reporter is credited.
The Co-Authored-By line references an AI tool (Claude Opus 5.5); it is credited as a tool rather than a human remediation developer.
x_patch2vuln.patchSummary: In app/View/Servers/preview_event.ctp, a regex check (preg_match against /^#[0-9a-f]{6}$/i) is added before the tag colour is used. If the colour does not match the hex pattern, it defaults to #ffffff. The validated $colour variable replaces the raw $tag['colour'] in both the background-color style property and the getTextColour() call, eliminating the untrusted value from the CSS context.
x_patch2vuln.cvssRationale: AV:N – the attack originates from a remote linked MISP server over the network. AC:L – no race conditions or special timing; simply setting a tag colour suffices. AT:N – no manipulation of the attack target is required. PR:L – the attacker needs low-privilege access (tag creation) on the linked server. UI:A – the victim must actively navigate to the event preview page. VC:N – no direct confidentiality loss on the vulnerable system. VI:N – no integrity impact on the vulnerable system's data. VA:N – no availability impact. SC:L – CSS injection may allow limited information disclosure on the client (e.g., reading page structure via CSS selectors or side channels). SI:L – the attacker can modify the visual presentation of the preview page (UI manipulation, overlay, spoofing). SA:N – no security authority impact.

capecRationale.rationale: The attack exploits the inherent trust between linked MISP instances. The local instance accepts and renders data (tag colours) from a remote linked server without sufficient validation, assuming the data is well-formed. The attacker leverages this trusted relationship to inject CSS. This is the closest CAPEC; no CAPEC specifically models CSS injection via trusted data sources, so CAPEC-66 is the best available match.

modelComparison.selectionNotice: The selected result is closest to model consensus; this heuristic does not establish factual correctness and human review remains required.

weaknessRationale.rationale: The tag colour value is not neutralized for the CSS context in which it is placed. HTML entity encoding (h()) does not sanitize CSS metacharacters such as semicolons, colons, or function calls, allowing CSS injection. CWE-74 is the most precise parent weakness covering injection into a downstream component (CSS) without a more specific child CWE for CSS injection.

descriptions.value:
MISP contains a CSS injection vulnerability in the remote event preview feature. When a user previews an event from a linked MISP server, the colour value associated with each remote tag is written directly into an inline CSS style attribute without sufficient validation. Although HTML entity encoding is applied, the value is interpreted as CSS within the style attribute, allowing a malicious or compromised linked server to inject arbitrary CSS declarations.

An attacker with the ability to create or modify tags on a linked MISP instance can craft a tag colour value containing CSS injection payloads. When a user on the local instance views the event preview, the injected CSS is rendered, potentially allowing UI manipulation, visual spoofing, or limited information disclosure through CSS-based techniques.

Preconditions:

- A linked MISP server relationship exists between the victim instance and the attacker-controlled instance.

- The attacker can create or modify tags on the linked server.

- A victim user views the remote event preview page.

Affected: <2.5.48.

cna.title: Vite: First 4 bytes of files outside of `server.fs` setting is exposed by `?vite-wasm-instance`

descriptions.value: Vite is a frontend tooling framework for JavaScript. From 8.2.0 until 8.2.4 and 8.3.3, the first 4 bytes of files outside of server.fs setting can be returned to the browser by a request containing ?vite-wasm-instance. Requests containing the ?vite-wasm-instance query are handled by the internal Wasm plugin's load hook. The hook removes the query and reads the resulting path directly from disk, but the server.fs checks were not applied. After reading the file, Vite attempts to parse it as WebAssembly. When that parse fails, Node and deno throws an error that contains the first 4 bytes of the file. This vulnerability is fixed in 8.2.4 and 8.3.3.

cna.title: Pillow: MSP RLE decoder expands a tiny file into unbounded memory

descriptions.value: Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 4.1.0 until 13.0.0, Pillow's MSP RLE decoder can expand a small file into an unbounded in-memory buffer. The decoder writes run-length output to BytesIO without limiting expansion to the declared image size. An attacker can supply a crafted MSP image to an application that loads its pixels. This can exhaust memory and deny service even when the declared pixel count passes the decompression-bomb check. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

cna.title: Pillow: TiffDecode returns uninitialized memory as pixels for short JPEG strips

descriptions.value: Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 5.3.0 until 13.0.0, Pillow can return uninitialized memory as pixels when libtiff performs a short decode of JPEG-compressed or Group 4 fax TIFF data. The _decodeStrip and _decodeTile buffers can be larger than the bytes written by libtiff, but Pillow converts the expected rows without clearing the unwritten tail. The tile path is affected from 5.3.0 and the strip path from 6.0.0. An attacker can supply a crafted TIFF to an application that loads and returns or re-encodes its pixels. This can disclose stale heap contents without memory corruption or a process crash. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Use after free in Animation in Google Chrome prior to 156.0.8078.47 allowed a remote attacker to execute arbitrary code inside the sandbox via a crafted HTML page. (Chromium security severity: Medium)

cna.title: Pillow: Double free in ImagingScaleAffine on calloc failure via Image.transform

descriptions.value: Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, Pillow can double free image memory when ImagingScaleAffine encounters a selective allocation failure. The affected fast path handles Transform.EXTENT or pure scale-and-translate Transform.AFFINE operations with the default NEAREST resampling. The output image allocation must succeed while the additional per-column lookup allocation fails, after which the error path deletes image storage that later cleanup releases again. An attacker who can drive such a large Image.transform() operation under memory pressure may trigger the failure. This can crash the process and may corrupt memory. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Performing a manipulation results in protection mechanism failure. Remote exploitation of the attack is possible. The attack is considered to have high complexity. The exploitability is assessed as difficult. Upgrading to version 6.2.4 is capable of addressing this issue. The patch is named 18fd12efa98a7d1977de7bdd379d8a848777b90f. Upgrading the affected component is recommended. The pre-requisite of the vulnerability is reflected by the CVSS vector. One of the project maintainers explains: "There is a real sandbox configuration issue here, but the report overstates it. The HTTP server defaults to http.sandbox=true, so commands received through /cmd temporarily enable cfg.sandbox. However, cfg.sandbox.grain defaults to all, which means all sandbox capabilities - including exec - remain allowed. Therefore enabling the HTTP sandbox alone does NOT prevent commands from spawning processes. This only matters when the HTTP command endpoint is reachable by someone you do not trust. It is not a remote vulnerability by default: the HTTP server must first be started and exposed to the attacker."

cna.title: Ghostscript: reintroduction of .charkeys -dsafer bypass in rhel 8

credits.value: Red Hat would like to thank Nicholas Pettas for reporting this issue.

workarounds.value:
Mitigation for this issue is either not available or the currently available options do not meet the Red Hat Product Security criteria comprising ease of use and deployment, applicability to widespread installation base, or stability.

--- CME Mitigation Guidance (2026-10-20) ---
Disclaimer: The following mitigation solutions are provided as a courtesy, pending the application of an official patch. This content was generated utilizing AI tools in conjunction with data from https://cmetaxonomy.org. Customers are advised to independently evaluate and test these temporary mitigations within their own infrastructure.

The highest-value action is to eliminate privileged .forceput operations in the .charkeys procedure to enforce -dSAFER sandbox boundaries: upgrade to the fixed Ghostscript builds, which replace .forceput invocations with standard put operations in the /.charkeys procedure in Resource/Init/gs_ttf.ps, closing all 2 injection vectors (crafted PostScript document, malicious TrueType font processing). Until patched, this is a concern on Ghostscript on Linux (RHEL 8) processing untrusted input, such as print or document-conversion services, so Restrict or halt processing of untrusted PostScript documents and TrueType font inputs across document-conversion and printing services that invoke Ghostscript. As a compensating measure, Use auditd to log unauthorized file access attempts and unexpected execve syscalls spawned by the Ghostscript process, Run SELinux in enforcing mode to confine the Ghostscript process to a restricted domain, Use Linux mount and PID namespaces to restrict filesystem and process visibility for Ghostscript execution, Deploy an EDR agent to detect and terminate unexpected shell or child process spawns from Ghostscript, and Use Falco or eBPF runtime security to detect anomalous child process execution and unauthorized file reads. These controls limit blast radius and contain exploitation, but they do not fix the underlying privileged .forceput sandbox bypass — apply the upstream patch to fully remediate.

Highest-impact CME: CME-1002 Audit Subsystem (auditd) (medium)

descriptions.value: A flaw was found in Ghostscript as shipped with Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8. The correction for CVE-2019-14869 was omitted during the rebase from version 9.25 to 9.27, leaving privileged .forceput operations in the .charkeys procedure insufficiently protected. Processing a specially crafted PostScript file may allow an attacker to bypass -dSAFER restrictions and access files outside the permitted paths or execute commands with the permissions of the Ghostscript process.

The attacker receives the status code and selected response headers, which allows probing of internal hosts and ports. Response bodies are not disclosed.

cna.title: Pillow: Infinite loop in MIC n_frames when the embedded TIFF

descriptions.value: Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 7.2.0 until 13.0.0, Pillow can enter an infinite loop while determining the frame count of a MIC image. MicImageFile inherits TIFF frame traversal, but MicImageFile.tell reports the OLE stream index and its seek() resets TIFF frame state, so an embedded TIFF with at least three IFDs never advances. When an application with olefile installed reads n_frames or saves all frames from a crafted MIC file, the non-advancing traversal can hold a worker at full CPU indefinitely. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

solutions.value: Apply upstream commit 7cf75587b6f38b87849fe192bf5dfd124b7702bc or a verified branch-specific backport. The fix requires the original IPv6 destination-prefix component to have offset zero before it can pass FlowSpec validation. The first fixed release has not yet been verified.

descriptions.value: An IPv6 FlowSpec validation bypass in the CZ.NIC BIRD Internet Routing Daemon allows an established BGP peer to inject FlowSpec rules matching destinations outside the address space authorized by the unicast-route validation procedure. With validation enabled on the receiving flow6 channel, BIRD fails to reject a destination prefix component with a nonzero offset, contrary to RFC 8956 section 5. It validates a reconstructed prefix with zero-filled skipped bits, although the original FlowSpec component can match a broader set of IPv6 addresses. Given a suitable unicast route from the peer, the rule can pass validation and, where export policy permits, be propagated to downstream peers. Downstream enforcement may cause unauthorized traffic filtering or redirection.

descriptions.description: CWE-1284 Improper Validation of Specified Quantity in Input

configurations.value: An established BGP peer must be able to send IPv6 FlowSpec to a receiving flow6 channel configured with "validate yes". A suitable unicast route from that peer must be present in the base table. Propagation additionally requires an export policy permitting the rule. Data-plane impact depends on downstream support for, acceptance of, and enforcement of the FlowSpec match and action.

x_patch2vuln.subject: fix: [html_to_markdown] block unspecified, shared, ULA and
x_patch2vuln.fixSummary: The fix extends the BLOCKED_RANGES list in is_safe_url() to include the previously missing IP address ranges: 0.0.0.0/8, 100.64.0.0/10, ::/128, fc00::/7, and fe80::/10. assumptions: PR:L assumes that creating or modifying a MISP attribute to trigger the html_to_markdown expansion module requires authenticated access. MISP typically enforces authentication for attribute operations, but the patch does not explicitly state the authentication model.

SC:H assumes the MISP server can reach internal services (e.g., cloud metadata at 169.254.169.254, internal admin panels, or CGNAT infrastructure) and that the responses are returned to the attacker via the Markdown conversion output. The actual impact depends on the server's network topology.
The exact affected version range is not specified in the patch. The nearest tag is v3.0.13 with 139 commits after the fix, but the precise release containing the fix is not identified.
CAPEC-12 is selected as the closest match; no alternative CAPEC more precisely describes an SSRF via incomplete IP-range validation in a URL-fetching module.

The patch does not indicate whether the module follows redirects to additional unblocked ranges; MAX_REDIRECTS is set to 10, and the redirect target validation is not shown in this patch. If redirect targets are not re-validated, the SSRF surface may be broader than what this patch addresses.
x_patch2vuln.patchSummary: In misp_modules/modules/expansion/html_to_markdown.py, five new ipaddress.ip_network() entries are added to the BLOCKED_RANGES list: 0.0.0.0/8, 100.64.0.0/10, ::/128, fc00::/7, and fe80::/10. In tests/test_html_to_markdown.py, two new test methods are added: test_blocks_unspecified_shared_ula_and_link_local_literals verifies that is_safe_url() returns False for literal URLs using each blocked range (including IPv4-mapped IPv6 forms), and test_blocks_hostnames_resolving_to_ula_addresses verifies that a hostname resolving to an fc00::/7 address is rejected.
x_patch2vuln.cvssRationale: AV:N: The vulnerable URL is supplied via a MISP attribute over the network. AC:L: Crafting a URL with a blocked-range IP is straightforward; no race or special timing is needed. AT:N: No manipulation of the target service is required. PR:L: Creating or modifying a MISP attribute that triggers the expansion module requires authenticated access (assumed; MISP typically requires authentication for attribute operations). UI:N: No victim interaction beyond the initial attribute creation is needed. VC:N, VI:N, VA:N: The MISP server itself is not compromised; it is used as a proxy. SC:H: The SSRF allows reading responses from internal services (e.g., cloud metadata endpoints, internal admin panels), representing a high confidentiality impact on the target system. SI:N, SA:N: The module performs a GET-style fetch for HTML-to-Markdown conversion; no evidence of write or security-impact on the target.

capecRationale.rationale: The patch directly addresses an SSRF condition: the application fetches a URL on behalf of the user, and the validation logic failed to block requests to internal and restricted IP ranges. An attacker crafts a URL with a blocked-range IP (e.g., http://0.0.0.0/admin or http://[fe80::1]/) to cause the MISP server to issue a request to an internal service. descriptions.value:
The html_to_markdown expansion module in MISP Modules contains a server-side request forgery (SSRF) vulnerability in its is_safe_url() URL validation function. The BLOCKED_RANGES list used to reject unsafe destination addresses was incomplete, omitting several critical IP address ranges. Specifically, the following ranges were not blocked: 0.0.0.0/8 (unspecified, which routes to loopback on Linux), 100.64.0.0/10 (carrier-grade NAT per RFC 6598), ::/128 (IPv6 unspecified), fc00::/7 (IPv6 Unique Local Addresses), and fe80::/10 (IPv6 link-local). The existing list only covered IPv4 loopback (127.0.0.0/8), RFC 1918 private ranges, IPv4 link-local (169.254.0.0/16), and IPv6 loopback (::1/128).

An authenticated user with the ability to create or modify MISP attributes that trigger the html_to_markdown expansion module could supply URLs pointing to these unblocked internal address ranges. Because the module fetches the URL server-side to convert HTML content to Markdown, the request is made from the MISP server's network context. This allows an attacker to probe and read responses from internal services, carrier-grade NAT infrastructure, or link-local endpoints that would otherwise be unreachable from external networks. IPv4-mapped IPv6 forms (e.g., [::ffff:0.0.0.0]) also bypassed the existing checks.

The security impact is primarily confidentiality: an attacker can read data served by internal services reachable from the MISP server. The MISP instance itself is not compromised, but it is abused as a proxy to access otherwise restricted network resources.

cna.title: webpack-dev-server vulnerable to cross-origin WebSocket access via proxied upgrades

descriptions.value: webpack-dev-server is a development server that provides live reloading for webpack projects. In versions before 5.2.7 and in version 6.0.0, when a proxy entry is configured to forward WebSockets, the server forwards non-HMR WebSocket upgrade requests to the proxy target without validating the Host or Origin headers, so the allowedHosts protection does not apply to those proxied upgrades. A malicious web page visited by a developer can open a cross-origin WebSocket through the dev server and read from and write to the proxied backend, even when the server is bound to loopback. The issue is fixed in webpack-dev-server 5.2.7 and 6.1.0, where proxied WebSocket upgrades pass the same Host and Origin validation as the HMR WebSocket, and users should upgrade to one of those versions or later. As a workaround, omit WebSocket forwarding from proxy entries that do not need it and scope the proxy to specific paths.

ai_annotations.description: Draft vulnerability metadata was generated from a git-format patch using an Ollama-hosted language model. Human validation is required before publication.

patches.subject: fix: [event] Remove every row belonging to an event when

x_patch2vuln.subject: fix: [event] Remove every row belonging to an event when
x_patch2vuln.fixSummary: The event deletion routine was extended to cascade-remove all associated child records that were previously left behind. Specifically, the fix ensures that event report tags, event graph rows, shadow attribute correlation rows (on both event_id and 1_event_id foreign keys), fuzzy ssdeep chunks, and attachment scan results are all purged within the same transaction as the parent event deletion, eliminating the orphaned-data condition.
assumptions: The affected version boundary is inferred from the tag_version_boundary metadata (v2.5.48 with 33 commits after fix); the exact fixed release version is not specified in the patch.

The CAPEC-126 mapping is the closest available match; the vulnerability is fundamentally an incomplete cleanup defect rather than a classic state-transition exploit, so the mapping carries uncertainty.

The confidentiality impact is assessed as None because the patch does not demonstrate that orphaned records are accessible to unauthorized users; the primary concern is data integrity and retention policy.
The commit message states the issue was 'found during the internal review, not externally reported,' so no external finder or reporter is credited.
The CVSS assumes the orphaned data is not directly queryable by other users through existing MISP endpoints; if such access paths exist, the confidentiality impact could be higher.
x_patch2vuln.patchSummary: In app/Model/Event.php, the quickDelete method was modified to: (1) add event_graph and shadow_attribute_correlations (both event_id and 1_event_id) to the relations array used for raw DELETE statements; (2) before executing the raw deletes, query for the IDs of event reports and for attribute/shadow-attribute IDs of type 'attachment' or 'malware-sample'; (3) delete EventReportTag rows matching those report IDs; (4) delete AttachmentScan rows matching those attribute IDs; (5) invoke FuzzyCorrelateSsdeep::purge() to remove ssdeep chunks for the event. All operations occur within the existing database transaction.
x_patch2vuln.cvssRationale: The vulnerability is in a web-based application (AV:N) and requires a straightforward authenticated action (AC:L, AT:N). Deleting events requires elevated privileges (PR:H). No user interaction is needed (UI:N). The primary impact is on the integrity of the vulnerable system's data store: orphaned records persist that should have been removed (VI:L). There is no direct confidentiality impact on the vulnerable system itself because the data was already accessible to the deleting user, and no evidence shows the orphans are exposed to other users (VC:N). No availability impact is demonstrated (VA:N). No impact on subsequent systems (SC:N, SI:N, SA:N).

capecRationale.rationale: The event object transitions to a 'deleted' state, but related child objects (report tags, correlations, scan results, ssdeep chunks) do not follow the expected state transition and remain in an active/persisted state. An attacker with delete privileges could exploit this by creating events with sensitive associated data, deleting the event, and then attempting to access the orphaned records through other application endpoints. This is the closest CAPEC to the observed incomplete state propagation; the mapping is uncertain because the primary issue is a maintenance/cleanup defect rather than a directly exploitable state machine flaw.

modelComparison.selectionNotice: The selected result is closest to model consensus; this heuristic does not establish factual correctness and human review remains required.

weaknessRationale.rationale: The event deletion logic failed to remove all associated child records (report tags, graphs, correlations, ssdeep chunks, scan results), leaving them as orphans in the database. This is a textbook incomplete cleanup of related resources when a parent object is destroyed.

descriptions.value:
MISP contains a data integrity flaw in its event deletion logic. When a user deletes an event, several associated records are not removed from the database, leaving them as orphaned entries. The affected record types include event report tags, event graph entries, proposal (shadow attribute) correlations, fuzzy ssdeep correlation chunks, and attachment scan results.

These orphaned records may contain sensitive threat intelligence data such as correlation mappings, scan results, and report metadata that should have been removed along with the parent event. Their persistence beyond the intended deletion lifecycle creates a risk of unintended data retention and potential information exposure if the records are reachable through other application queries or administrative interfaces.

Preconditions:

- An authenticated user with sufficient privileges to delete events in MISP.

- The event must have associated reports, graphs, correlations, ssdeep chunks, or attachment scan results.

Impact:

- Residual sensitive data persists in the database after the parent event is deleted.

- Accumulation of orphaned records over time may contribute to storage bloat.

- Orphaned records may be inadvertently exposed through other data-access paths that do not validate the existence of the parent event.

Affected versions: <2.5.48

cna.title: Pillow: Heap use-after-free when encoding TIFF to an in-memory buffer

descriptions.value: Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 11.3.0 until 13.0.0, Pillow has a heap use-after-free when libtiff rejects a tag while encoding TIFF data to an in-memory buffer. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

cna.title: MISP Proposal ACL Bypass: Incomplete Distribution Level Check in Shadow Attribute Access Control

ai_annotations.description: Draft vulnerability metadata was generated from a git-format patch using an Ollama-hosted language model. Human validation is required before publication.

patches.subject: fix: [proposals] Apply the attribute ACL rules to proposals

x_patch2vuln.subject: fix: [proposals] Apply the attribute ACL rules to proposals
x_patch2vuln.fixSummary: The fix enforces the distribution level constraint in the sharing group access check, requiring distribution level 4 (All communities) for the sharing group test to apply. Additionally, the owning organisation is now explicitly granted access to proposals on its own attributes regardless of distribution level, correcting the over-restrictive behavior.
assumptions: The CAPEC mapping (CAPEC-2, Parameter Tampering) is the closest available match but is uncertain; the vulnerability is more accurately a missing authorization check (incomplete ACL evaluation) rather than active parameter manipulation by the attacker.
The affected version boundary is inferred from the tag v2.5.48 and the commit position (35 commits after the fix); exact version boundaries are not explicitly stated in the patch metadata.

The second aspect of the vulnerability (owner organisation denied access to its own proposals) is primarily a functional/availability defect rather than a security vulnerability, but is included as part of the same fix and the same root cause (incomplete ACL logic).
CVSS PR:L assumes the attacker must be an authenticated MISP user with membership in a relevant sharing group; no evidence supports unauthenticated access.
The Co-Authored-By line credits an AI assistant (Claude Opus 5.5) as a remediation developer; this is recorded as-is from the commit metadata.
x_patch2vuln.patchSummary: In the shadow attribute model's condition builder, the sharing group check for both objects and attributes now includes an AND condition requiring distribution = 4 alongside the sharing_group_id IN check. The attribute distribution condition was changed from a simple sharing_group_id IN clause to a compound AND condition with distribution = 4. A new OR condition (Event.org_id matching the user's org_id) was added to grant the owning organisation access to proposals on its own attributes.
x_patch2vuln.cvssRationale: AV:N: MISP is a network-accessible web application. AC:L: The user only needs to be a member of a sharing group; no special conditions or race conditions are required. AT:N: No active attack requirements beyond normal API usage. PR:L: The attacker must be an authenticated user with membership in a relevant sharing group. UI:N: No user interaction is required; the check is server-side. VC:H: The user can view proposals (proposed attribute changes) that should be restricted by distribution level, disclosing sensitive information about proposed changes. VI:N: No integrity impact; the user cannot modify proposals. VA:N: No availability impact. SC/SI/SA:N: No impact on subsequent components.

capecRationale.rationale: The user's sharing group membership (a parameter of their identity/session) was leveraged by the flawed authorization logic to grant access to proposals without the required distribution level check. This is the closest available CAPEC pattern; the user is not actively tampering with parameters, but the system improperly treats group membership as a sufficient access parameter without enforcing the additional distribution constraint. The mapping is uncertain because the vulnerability is more accurately a missing authorization check than active parameter manipulation.

modelComparison.selectionNotice: The selected result is closest to model consensus; this heuristic does not establish factual correctness and human review remains required.

weaknessRationale.rationale: The authorization check for proposal visibility was missing the distribution level constraint. The system evaluated sharing group membership as sufficient for access without also requiring the distribution level to be 4 (All communities), resulting in an incomplete authorization check that allowed access to proposals on more restrictively distributed attributes.

descriptions.value: CAPEC-2 Parameter Tampering

solutions.value: The fix enforces the distribution level constraint in the sharing group access check, requiring distribution level 4 (All communities) for the sharing group test to apply. Additionally, the owning organisation is now explicitly granted access to proposals on its own attributes regardless of distribution level, correcting the over-restrictive behavior.

Additionally, the owning organisation is now explicitly granted access to proposals on its own attributes regardless of distribution level, correcting the over-restrictive behavior.

descriptions.value:
MISP contains an access control flaw in the proposal (shadow attribute) visibility logic. The authorization check accepted any attribute or object carrying one of the user's sharing groups without verifying the distribution level, and denied the owning organisation access to proposals on its own organisation-only attributes.

- A user belonging to a sharing group could view proposals on attributes or objects with that sharing group, regardless of the attribute's distribution level (levels 1-3 should restrict visibility)

- The owning organisation could not view proposals on its own org-only attributes

Security impact: Unauthorized disclosure of proposed attribute changes to users who should not have access based on distribution level restrictions.

Affected: <2.5.48

credits.value: Red Hat would like to thank D.M Sithum Vihanga for reporting this issue.

workarounds.value:
Disable the rhc-canonical-facts timer to prevent automatic triggering of the vulnerable service:

    systemctl stop rhc-canonical-facts.timer
    systemctl disable rhc-canonical-facts.timer

Note that this will prevent rhc from updating canonical facts automatically. The rhc connect command will still trigger the service manually.

The service runs as root and operates on a file inside a directory owned by an unprivileged system user without verifying that the file is not a symbolic link. A local attacker who has already compromised the privileged yggdrasil system service account can exploit this to gain ownership of arbitrary files, leading to privilege escalation to root.

cna.title: MISP Event Synchronization Exposes Non-Exportable Tags on Remote Instances

ai_annotations.description: Draft vulnerability metadata was generated from a git-format patch using an Ollama-hosted language model. Human validation is required before publication.

patches.subject: fix: [sync] Filter the tags of every event report pushed to a

x_patch2vuln.subject: fix: [sync] Filter the tags of every event report pushed to a
x_patch2vuln.fixSummary: The non-exportable tag filtering is now invoked for each individual event report within the iteration loop, ensuring that restricted tags are removed from every report before it is transmitted to the remote MISP instance. This prevents the leakage of tags that were explicitly marked as non-exportable.
assumptions: The affected version boundary is inferred from the tag_version_boundary metadata (v2.5.48 with 34 commits after fix), suggesting the fix is included in v2.5.48 and prior versions are affected. No explicit version range is stated in the patch.
PR:L assumes that a non-admin authenticated user with push-to-remote permissions can trigger the sync; if only administrators can initiate sync, PR should be raised to H.
The CAPEC-128 mapping is uncertain; no CAPEC pattern precisely describes a per-item filtering logic error causing data leakage during a legitimate operation.
The security impact is assessed as limited to tag disclosure; the actual sensitivity of 'non-exportable' tags depends on MISP deployment configuration and is not specified in the patch.
The availability impact (null report push causing remote save failure) is considered minor and not reflected in the CVSS vector as the primary concern is information disclosure.
x_patch2vuln.patchSummary: In app/Model/Event.php, the call to __removeNonExportableTags was moved from a single post-loop invocation (which used the last $key value from the foreach) into the else branch of the loop body, so it executes for each non-empty report individually. The post-loop else block that applied the filter to a single report was removed, eliminating both the tag-leakage bug and the null-report push when the last report was empty.
x_patch2vuln.cvssRationale: AV:N: The vulnerability is triggered over the network during MISP-to-MISP synchronization. AC:L: No special conditions are needed beyond a configured sync relationship and an event with multiple reports. AT:N: No attacker interaction is required; the bug triggers on any sync push. PR:L: An authenticated user with permission to push events to a remote server is required. UI:N: No user interaction beyond initiating the sync. VC:L: Non-exportable tags (restricted metadata) are disclosed to the remote instance; the core event data is not exposed. VI:N, VA:N: No integrity or availability impact on the local instance. SC:N, SI:N, SA:N: No impact on the remote instance's confidentiality, integrity, or availability beyond receiving the tags it should not have.

capecRationale.rationale: This is the closest available CAPEC pattern. The vulnerability arises from a code logic error that causes data (non-exportable tags) to be improperly exposed during a legitimate sync operation. The mapping is uncertain because the issue is a logic bug in data filtering rather than a deliberate attacker action; no CAPEC pattern precisely covers 'improper per-item filtering in a loop causing data leakage during a legitimate API operation.'

modelComparison.selectionNotice: The selected result is closest to model consensus; this heuristic does not establish factual correctness and human review remains required.

weaknessRationale.rationale: Tags explicitly marked as non-exportable were not filtered from event reports during synchronization, exposing restricted information to the remote MISP instance. The root cause is a logic error (filter applied once instead of per-item), but the security consequence is information disclosure.

solutions.value: The non-exportable tag filtering is now invoked for each individual event report within the iteration loop, ensuring that restricted tags are removed from every report before it is transmitted to the remote MISP instance. This prevents the leakage of tags that were explicitly marked as non-exportable.

supportingMedia.value: The non-exportable tag filtering is now invoked for each individual event report within the iteration loop, ensuring that restricted tags are removed from every report before it is transmitted to the remote MISP instance. This prevents the leakage of tags that were explicitly marked as non-exportable.

descriptions.value:
In MISP, the event synchronization process contained a logic error in the preparation of event reports for remote push. The filtering of non-exportable tags was applied only once after the iteration over all reports, rather than to each individual report.

As a result:

- All reports except the last one in the set were pushed to the remote MISP instance with their non-exportable tags intact, effectively disclosing restricted tag information to the receiving instance.

- When the last report in the set was withheld (empty), a null report was pushed, causing the remote instance to fail saving the event.

This issue affects any MISP instance configured to push events with multiple reports to a remote server via synchronization.

Affected: <2.5.48.

supportingMedia.value:
In MISP, the event synchronization process contained a logic error in the preparation of event reports for remote push. The filtering of non-exportable tags was applied only once after the iteration over all reports, rather than to each individual report.

As a result:

- All reports except the last one in the set were pushed to the remote MISP instance with their non-exportable tags intact, effectively disclosing restricted tag information to the receiving instance.

- When the last report in the set was withheld (empty), a null report was pushed, causing the remote instance to fail saving the event.

This issue affects any MISP instance configured to push events with multiple reports to a remote server via synchronization.

Affected: <2.5.48.

descriptions.value: Vite is a frontend tooling framework for JavaScript. Prior to 6.4.4, 7.3.7, 8.1.6, 8.2.4, and 8.3.3, import analysis can record a root-relative browser URL in safeModulePaths instead of the cleaned resolved module identifier. On a network-accessible, non-Windows development server, an imported project file whose URL matches an absolute host path can authorize a later raw-filesystem request for that host file, provided server.fs.deny does not block it. The request can disclose the matching file outside the project root, but it does not allow arbitrary path traversal because the host path must correspond to a project-relative URL authorized by the application graph. This issue is fixed in versions 6.4.4, 7.3.7, 8.1.6, 8.2.4, and 8.3.3.

cna.title: Pillow: Heap buffer overflow in _tiffWriteProc when saving TIFF to BytesIO

descriptions.value: Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 2.0.0 until 13.0.0, Pillow has a heap buffer overflow and stale-heap disclosure in _tiffWriteProc when saving compressed TIFF data through libtiff to a target without a usable fileno(), such as BytesIO. The callback sizes its allocation from the prior buffer size instead of the current write position, allowing an attacker-controlled out-of-line TIFF tag or retained ICC profile to be copied beyond the allocation after libtiff seeks forward. This overflow can crash the process and may allow code execution. Independently, unwritten alignment gaps in compressed TIFF output larger than 64 KiB can disclose stale heap bytes without a crafted tag. File paths and targets with real file descriptors are unaffected. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

cna.title: Pillow: Quadratic GIF comment copying during save

descriptions.value: Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 9.2.0 until 13.0.0, Pillow performs quadratic copying when saving a GIF with a long comment. _get_global_header() repeatedly copies portions of comment data while assembling the global header, including comments retained from an untrusted input image. An attacker can supply an image with a large GIF comment to an application that saves it as GIF. This can consume excessive CPU and delay or deny service. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

cna.title: Captcha Bypass in extension "Accessible Form Captcha" (bw_captcha)

descriptions.value: The extension hides the correct answer to each CAPTCHA inside the image data of the CAPTCHA itself. Anyone who can request a CAPTCHA image can read the answer from it and submit it, so automated clients can pass the challenge. ai_annotations.description: Draft vulnerability metadata was generated from a git-format patch using an Ollama-hosted language model. Human validation is required before publication.

patches.subject: fix: [workflows] Escape misp-module parameter names used as

x_patch2vuln.subject: fix: [workflows] Escape misp-module parameter names used as
x_patch2vuln.fixSummary: The fix applies HTML output encoding (the h() helper) to the parameter name before it is used as a form label, ensuring that any HTML metacharacters in the value are neutralized and rendered as inert text rather than executable markup.
assumptions: The misp-modules service is assumed to be a component whose output can be influenced by a module developer or a compromised service endpoint; the exact attack vector for injecting a malicious parameter name is not detailed in the patch.
MISP requires authentication to access the workflow module page; PR:L is assumed based on MISP's standard access model.
The affected version boundary (< 2.5.48) is inferred from the tag_version_boundary metadata (v2.5.48, 25 commits after fix); the exact first affected version is not specified.
CAPEC-1 (Reflected XSS) is the closest match; the data source is a backend service rather than a direct request parameter, but the unencoded reflection into HTML is the defining characteristic.
The h() function is assumed to be CakePHP's HTML-encoding helper (equivalent to htmlspecialchars), based on the framework context of the MISP codebase.
x_patch2vuln.patchSummary: In app/Model/WorkflowModules/Module_misp_module.php, the translateParams method was modified: the 'label' array element changed from Inflector::humanize($paramName) to h(Inflector::humanize($paramName)), wrapping the humanized parameter name in CakePHP's HTML-encoding function before it is assigned as a form label.
x_patch2vuln.cvssRationale: AV:N – web-based, reachable over the network. AC:L – no race or special timing; the misp-modules service simply needs to return a crafted parameter name. AT:N – no manipulation of the target system required. PR:L – the victim must be an authenticated MISP user to view the workflow module page. UI:A – the victim must actively load the workflow module page for the script to execute. VC/VI/VA:N – the MISP server itself is not compromised. SC:L – the attacker can read cookies or session data in the victim's browser. SI:L – the attacker can modify the page or perform actions in the victim's session. SA:N – no elevation of security authority on the server.

capecRationale.rationale: The misp-modules service supplies parameter names that are reflected into the HTML of the workflow module page without encoding. The attacker-controlled data flows from an external source into the rendered output, matching the reflected XSS pattern. Uncertainty: the data originates from a backend service rather than a direct HTTP parameter, but the effect (untrusted data reflected into HTML without encoding) is functionally identical to reflected XSS.

modelComparison.selectionNotice: The selected result is closest to model consensus; this heuristic does not establish factual correctness and human review remains required.

weaknessRationale.rationale: The parameter name from an external service is inserted into HTML output (a form label) without HTML encoding, allowing injected markup or script to execute in the victim's browser. This is a textbook reflected XSS.

descriptions.value:
MISP contains a reflected cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability in the workflow module interface. Parameter names returned by the misp-modules service are rendered as raw HTML form labels on the workflow module page without output encoding. An attacker who can influence the parameter names reported by the misp-modules service can inject arbitrary HTML or JavaScript that executes in the context of an authenticated MISP user's browser.

Preconditions:

- The attacker must be able to control or influence parameter names reported by the misp-modules service.

- A victim must be authenticated and view the affected workflow module page.

Impact:

- Execution of arbitrary JavaScript in the victim's browser session.

- Potential theft of session tokens, manipulation of the MISP interface, or initiation of unauthorized actions on behalf of the victim.

Affected versions: <2.5.48.

descriptions.value: VideoLAN libbluray through 1.5.1 contains an out-of-bounds read vulnerability in clpi_access_point() that allows attackers to crash applications by supplying a ClipInfo file with an empty EP-map fine table.
